title: Cyflwyniadau
subtitle: Greetings & Everyday Pleasantries
description: Master natural North Welsh greetings, departures, and asking how people are doing.

phrases.notes: Standard morning greeting used universally across Wales.
Often contracted casually in the North to 'Sut ti?' or 'Su'mai?'.
Notice the 'ch' sound in 'chithau'—aspirated voiceless velar fricative like Scottish 'loch'.
In North Wales 'ydy' is typically used for 'is' where South Wales frequently uses 'yw'.
Traditional North Welsh farewell, shortened from 'Duw a fo gyda chwi'.
Features 'rŵan' (now), the quintessential Northern indicator.

title: Cymraeg y Gogledd
subtitle: Key Northern Dialect Words
description: Learn the hallmark Northern words that instantly distinguish Gogledd speech from the South.

phrases.notes: 'Be'' is short for 'Beth'. 'Rŵan' is exclusively North Welsh (Southern: 'nawr').
'Efo' means 'with' (Southern: 'gyda'). 'Fo' means 'him' (Southern: 'fe').
phrases.dialectFocus: efo (with) vs gyda, fo vs fe

phrases.notes: 'Dallt' is the common Northern verb for understand (Southern: 'deall'). Notice the final 'll' sound.

phrases.welsh: Dw i ddim yn dallt o.
phrases.phonetic: DOO ee THEEM un DAH-llt oh.
phrases.notes: 'O' is used in the North for both 'him' and masculine 'it' where the South uses 'e'.
North Wales often uses 'Lle' directly for 'Where' instead of 'Ble'.
A daily weather phrase featuring Northern 'rŵan'.

title: Anghenion a Dymuniadau
subtitle: Wants, Needs & Having
description: Expressing desire and possession using Northern idioms like 'isio', 'paned', and 'gen i'.

phrases.welsh: Dw i isio paned o de.
phrases.english: I want a cup of tea.
phrases.phonetic: DOO ee EES-yoh PAH-ned oh DEH.
phrases.notes: 'Isio' (want) is the classic Northern spoken form. 'Paned' is Northern for a cuppa (South: 'dishgled').
phrases.dialectFocus: isio vs eisiau/moyn, paned vs dishgled

phrases.notes: Northern possession pattern: 'gynnoch chi' instead of Southern 'gyda chi'.

phrases.welsh: Oes, mae gen i goffi poeth.
phrases.phonetic: OYS, my GEN ee GOH-fee POYTH.
phrases.notes: 'Mae gen i' (I have) is Northern. The South says 'Mae gyda fi'.

phrases.welsh: Dw i'n dysgu Cymraeg y Gogledd.
phrases.phonetic: DOO een DUHS-gee kum-RYE-g uh GOG-leth.
phrases.notes: 'Cymraeg y Gogledd' specifically means the Welsh of the North.
'Braf' is frequently used in conversational Welsh for pleasant/fine/lovely.

title: Labordy Ynganu
subtitle: Pronunciation Clinic: Tricky Northern Sounds
description: Targeted practice for authentic Welsh sounds: LL, CH, the Northern 'U' vowel, and trilled R.

phrases.english: St Mary's church by the pool
phrases.notes: The iconic 'LL' sound: place the tip of your tongue firmly against the ridge behind your upper teeth, then gently blow air around the sides without vibrating your vocal cords.
Features two 'CH' sounds [x]. Friction is produced at the soft palate / uvula like German 'Bach' or Scottish 'loch'.
In North Wales, the letter 'u' (and 'y' in monosyllables like 'tŷ') represents a high central unrounded vowel [ɨ], produced with the tongue slightly further back than English 'ee'.
Combines a trilled 'r', the voiced dental fricative 'dd' [ð] (like 'th' in 'this'), and final 'ch'.
